meta.note: Original CISSP-style practice questions. matching questions carry a prompts[] (left items numbered 1..n) and options[] (right items A..n); correct_answer encodes the pairing. sequence_ordering correct_answer lists option labels in correct order.

questions.question: Running software in an isolated environment that restricts its access to system resources to avoid unintended interactions is known as:

explanation.why_correct: Confinement (sandboxing) runs software in an isolated environment, restricting its access to system resources to prevent unintended interactions.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Transitive trust is when trust is passed along a chain of relationships.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Open design means the design can be openly reviewed; security rests on secret keys.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Psychological acceptability concerns making security usable.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of confinement/sandboxing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Concepts

questions.question: A control that limits the memory resources available to a process so it cannot affect other areas of the system is referred to as:

explanation.why_correct: Bounds limit the memory/resources available to a process, ensuring it operates within assigned limits and cannot impact other system areas.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Assurance is the degree of confidence that security controls work as intended.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Complete mediation requires authorization on every access.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Work factor measures the effort required to break a control or cipher.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes bounds (resource limits) from related concepts.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Concepts

questions.question: System A trusts System B, and System B trusts System C. Because of this chain, System A effectively trusts System C even though it was never directly evaluated. This relationship is an example of:

explanation.why_correct: Transitive trust is when trust flows along a chain (A→B→C), causing A to implicitly trust C; least common mechanism warns against such transitive trust.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Complete mediation checks authorization on every access, not chained trust.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Separation of duties splits critical functions among people.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fail-safe defaults deny by default; unrelated to trust chaining.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recognizing transitive trust and its inherent risk.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Trust and Secure Design

questions.question: In secure design, "assurance" refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: The act of isolating a process in memory

options.label: B
options.text: A precomputed table of password hashes

options.label: C
options.text: The degree of confidence that a system's security controls function as intended

options.label: D
options.text: A magnetic method of destroying data

explanation.why_correct: Assurance is the level of confidence that security measures/controls work correctly and as intended.

why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes memory protection/isolation.
why_others_are_wrong.B: That describes a rainbow table.
why_others_are_wrong.D: That describes degaussing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the assurance concept.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Trust and Secure Design

questions.question: A design principle stating that default settings should DENY access and that components should fail closed rather than open is:

explanation.why_correct: Fail-safe defaults require that default settings deny access and that components fail securely (closed) rather than open.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Open design means the design itself is open to review.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Psychological acceptability concerns usability of security.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Economy of mechanism favors simple, small designs.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps deny-by-default/fail-closed to fail-safe defaults.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: Which principle requires that authorization be checked EVERY time a subject requests access to an object, rather than once and cached indefinitely?

explanation.why_correct: Complete mediation requires authorization to be verified on each access request, preventing unauthorized access that could arise from stale permissions.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Least common mechanism limits shared components/transitive trust.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Economy of mechanism favors simplicity.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Open design concerns openness of the design to review.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of complete mediation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: The "open design" principle holds that the security of a system should depend on:

options.label: B
options.text: Keeping the entire system design secret from everyone

options.label: C
options.text: Avoiding any external review of the system

options.label: D
options.text: Keeping cryptographic keys and passwords secret, not on hiding the design itself

explanation.why_correct: Open design states the design should be open to external review; security should rest on secret keys/passwords, not obscurity of the design (the opposite of security through obscurity).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Hiding the design is security through obscurity, which open design rejects.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Proprietary undisclosed algorithms contradict open design.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Open design encourages external review.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests open design vs. security through obscurity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: Which secure design principle favors keeping a design as simple and small as possible to reduce complexity and potential errors?

explanation.why_correct: Economy of mechanism calls for simple, small designs to reduce complexity and the likelihood of errors/flaws.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Least privilege grants minimum necessary access.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Complete mediation checks every access.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Separation of privilege requires multiple subjects for critical functions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of economy of mechanism.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: A principle that advises LIMITING shared components and avoiding transitive trust between processes to minimize cross-system vulnerabilities is:

explanation.why_correct: Least common mechanism minimizes shared mechanisms/components and avoids transitive trust, reducing pathways for cross-system compromise.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Psychological acceptability concerns usable security.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fail-safe defaults deny by default.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Complete mediation checks authorization on each access.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes least common mechanism from other principles.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: Designing security features so users find them simple and are not tempted to bypass them embodies which principle?

explanation.why_correct: Psychological acceptability holds that security should be user-friendly so users do not circumvent it through error or frustration.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Economy of mechanism is about design simplicity, not user experience.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Open design concerns openness of design to review.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Separation of privilege requires multiple parties for critical actions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps usable security to psychological acceptability.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: Requiring two or more subjects to execute a critical function, minimizing risk from any single user, is the principle of:

explanation.why_correct: Separation of privilege (separation of duties) requires two or more subjects to perform critical functions, reducing single-user risk.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Least privilege limits each subject to minimum access, but does not require multiple subjects for one function.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Least common mechanism limits shared components.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Complete mediation checks every access.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes separation of privilege from least privilege.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are among Saltzer and Schroeder's secure design principles? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Least privilege and complete mediation are Saltzer & Schroeder design principles.

why_others_are_wrong.A: "No write down" is the Bell-LaPadula star property, not a Saltzer-Schroeder design principle.
why_others_are_wrong.B: "Birthday attack resistance" is a cryptographic property, not a design principle.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates Saltzer-Schroeder principles from model rules and crypto concepts.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: The central premise of Zero Trust Architecture is:

options.label: A
options.text: Only perimeter firewalls are needed for security

options.label: B
options.text: Never automatically trust any user or device; verify every access on a per-session basis

options.label: C
options.text: Trust all devices on the internal/private network by default

options.label: D
options.text: Trust is granted permanently after the first successful login

explanation.why_correct: Zero Trust assumes no implicit trust—every access is authenticated/authorized per session regardless of network location.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Zero Trust explicitly rejects implicit trust of private networks.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Access is evaluated continuously per session, not granted permanently.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Zero Trust goes beyond perimeter defenses to per-resource verification.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the no-implicit-trust premise of ZT.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Zero Trust Architecture

questions.question: Which document defines the Zero Trust Architecture principles referenced in the guide?

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-207 defines Zero Trust Architecture principles.

why_others_are_wrong.D: NIST SP 800-53 is the security/privacy control catalog.
why_others_are_wrong.B: ISO 11889 is the TPM standard.
why_others_are_wrong.C: NIST SP 800-88 covers media sanitization.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps Zero Trust to NIST SP 800-207.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Principles

questions.question: In a Zero Trust Architecture, which component actually ENFORCES the access decision by acting as a gateway between a subject and a resource?

explanation.why_correct: The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) enforces access control by acting as the gateway/intermediary between subjects and resources.

why_others_are_wrong.C: The Policy Engine decides whether to grant access (the decision), but does not enforce at the gateway.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The Policy Administrator manages communication and token creation between the PE and PEP.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A TPM is a cryptographic hardware chip, not a ZT policy component.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes PEP (enforce) from PE (decide) and PA (manage).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Zero Trust Architecture Components

questions.question: Match each Zero Trust component (1-3) to its role (A-C).

options.label: A
options.text: Enforces access as a gateway/intermediary between subject and resource

options.label: B
options.text: Manages subject-resource communication and creates access tokens

options.label: C
options.text: Decides whether to authorize a subject's access to a resource and logs decisions

explanation.why_correct: Policy Engine → decides/logs (B); Policy Administrator → manages communication/tokens (A); Policy Enforcement Point → enforces at the gateway (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the decide/manage/enforce split of ZT components.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Zero Trust Architecture Components

questions.question: An organization currently grants broad network access once a device connects to the corporate LAN. To move toward Zero Trust, it should:

options.label: A
options.text: Grant permanent access tokens that never expire

options.label: B
options.text: Continue trusting all LAN-connected devices to reduce friction

options.label: C
options.text: Treat the internal network as untrusted and authenticate/authorize each resource request

options.label: D
options.text: Rely solely on a stronger perimeter firewall

explanation.why_correct: Zero Trust removes implicit trust of private networks—each resource request is authenticated/authorized regardless of network location.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Trusting LAN devices by default is exactly what Zero Trust eliminates.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A stronger perimeter still leaves implicit internal trust intact.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Non-expiring tokens contradict per-session, continuous verification.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests applying Zero Trust to remove implicit internal trust.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Zero Trust Architecture

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model, an organization that uses a cloud provider typically INHERITS which type of control from the provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Physical security of the data center

explanation.why_correct: Customers inherit controls like physical security of the provider's data centers, while retaining responsibility for their own data and access.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Data classification remains the customer's responsibility.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Access reviews of the customer's users remain the customer's job.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Application input validation is the customer's responsibility (especially in IaaS/PaaS).

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies physical security as a commonly inherited control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Shared Responsibility Model

questions.question: The Privacy by Design principle "Proactive, not Reactive" means an organization should:

options.label: A
options.text: Wait for a breach before adding any privacy controls

options.label: B
options.text: Collect as much data as possible by default

options.label: C
options.text: Disclose user data publicly for transparency

options.label: D
options.text: Anticipate and prevent privacy risks before they occur rather than responding after the fact

explanation.why_correct: Proactive, not reactive focuses on anticipating and preventing privacy risks before they materialize, aiming beyond mere compliance.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Waiting for a breach is reactive—the opposite of this principle.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Collecting maximal data violates privacy by default/data minimization.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Transparency means clear policies, not exposing user data publicly.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the proactive, preventative stance of Privacy by Design.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Privacy By Design

questions.question: A new app is configured so that, out of the box, it shares the minimum data necessary and keeps the strictest privacy settings unless a user opts in to more sharing. This best reflects which Privacy by Design principle?

explanation.why_correct: Privacy by Default sets the strictest privacy protections as the default, collecting only necessary data and limiting purpose, scope, and retention.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Visibility and Transparency concerns publishing accessible privacy policies.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Full Functionality (Positive-Sum) balances privacy with functionality without trade-offs.
why_others_are_wrong.D: End-to-End Security protects data across its full lifecycle.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps default-minimal-sharing to Privacy by Default.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Privacy By Design

questions.question: The "Full Functionality – Positive-Sum, Not Zero-Sum" principle asserts that privacy measures should:

options.label: A
options.text: Replace all business functionality with privacy controls

options.label: B
options.text: Coexist with business objectives and usability rather than forcing an either/or trade-off

options.label: C
options.text: Be applied only after the product is decommissioned

options.label: D
options.text: Always be sacrificed to maximize functionality

explanation.why_correct: Positive-sum means privacy protections support business processes and user experience without unnecessary trade-offs—not an either/or choice.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Sacrificing privacy for functionality is the zero-sum view this principle rejects.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Privacy does not replace functionality; the two coexist.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Privacy is integrated throughout, not only at decommission.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the positive-sum (no trade-off) principle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Full Functionality – Positive-Sum, Not Zero-Sum

questions.question: The PRIMARY goal of memory protection as a system security capability is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the clock speed of the CPU

options.label: B
options.text: Provide physical access control to the data center

options.label: C
options.text: Prevent processes in memory from interacting with each other to avoid data leaks

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypt all network traffic in transit

explanation.why_correct: Memory protection prevents processes in memory from interacting, allowing multiple processes (even at different security levels) to run independently without data leakage.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Memory protection is about isolation, not CPU performance.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Encrypting network traffic is a transport-layer control, not memory protection.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Physical access control is a facility control, not memory protection.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps process isolation in memory to memory protection.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > System Security Capabilities

questions.question: An application hides admin-only menu items from standard users, exposing only the functions appropriate to each role. This capability is a:

explanation.why_correct: A restricted/constrained interface limits the objects and functions a user can access based on privilege level, implementing least privilege at the UI.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A TPM is a cryptographic hardware chip.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A reference monitor mediates all access between subjects and objects at a system level.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A covert channel is an unauthorized communication path, not a UI control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps role-based UI hiding to constrained interfaces.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > User Interfaces (Restricted or Constrained Interfaces)

questions.question: A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is BEST described as:

options.label: A
options.text: A software sandbox for running untrusted code

options.label: B
options.text: A specialized motherboard chip that provides cryptographic services such as key generation and encryption

options.label: C
options.text: A network appliance that filters egress traffic

options.label: D
options.text: A cloud service that stores virtual machines

explanation.why_correct: A TPM is a specialized motherboard chip (ISO 11889) providing cryptographic services such as creating key pairs, signing data, and encryption.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A TPM is local hardware, not a cloud VM service.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Egress filtering is a network DLP/firewall function.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A sandbox isolates code in software, not a cryptographic chip.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the TPM as a cryptographic hardware chip.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Trusted Platform Module (TPM)

questions.question: Which TPM component is a private key embedded by the hardware manufacturer that is unique and cannot be altered?

explanation.why_correct: The Endorsement Key (EK) is a private key embedded by the hardware manufacturer that is unalterable and unique to the TPM.

why_others_are_wrong.B: The Storage Root Key (SRK) secures keys stored in the TPM.
why_others_are_wrong.D: PCRs track the current software/configuration state.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The AIK is used for attestation of platform identity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes the manufacturer-embedded EK from other TPM components.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Trusted Platform Module (TPM)

questions.question: A standalone cryptographic device used to perform encryption/decryption and securely manage cryptographic keys for high-security applications is a:

explanation.why_correct: An HSM is a standalone cryptographic device providing encryption/decryption and high-security key management.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A PEP enforces Zero Trust access decisions.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A constrained interface limits UI functions by privilege.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A sandbox isolates running code.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes HSM (standalone crypto device) from a TPM (motherboard chip).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Trusted Platform Module (TPM)

questions.question: As a system security capability, virtualization is useful for malware analysis primarily because it:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminates the need for any access controls

options.label: B
options.text: Encrypts all data on the network

options.label: C
options.text: Provides isolated, sandboxed environments where malware can run without affecting the host

options.label: D
options.text: Permanently prevents all malware from executing

explanation.why_correct: Virtualization enables isolated, sandboxed environments useful for safely analyzing malware, along with centralized control, scalability, and easy recovery.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Virtualization isolates malware but does not prevent its execution within the sandbox.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Virtualization is about emulating systems, not encrypting network traffic.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Access controls are still required in virtualized environments.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects virtualization isolation to safe malware analysis.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > System Security Capabilities

questions.question: Granting a subject only the minimum access required to perform its job functions is the principle of:

explanation.why_correct: Least privilege grants subjects only the minimum access necessary for their functions.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Open design concerns openness of the design to review.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Economy of mechanism favors simple design.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Complete mediation checks authorization on each access.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of least privilege as a design principle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Secure Design Principles

questions.question: Which TWO statements reflect NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust principles? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Authentication and authorization are strictly enforced before access is allowed

options.label: B
options.text: Devices on the private network are implicitly trusted

options.label: C
options.text: Once authenticated, a session is trusted indefinitely

options.label: D
options.text: Access to resources is granted on a per-session basis

explanation.why_correct: Per-session access and strict, real-time authentication/authorization are core NIST SP 800-207 principles.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Zero Trust grants no implicit trust to private-network devices.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Trust is continuously evaluated, not granted indefinitely.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates genuine Zero Trust principles from implicit-trust distractors.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Principles

questions.question: The Privacy by Design principle of "End-to-End Security – Full Lifecycle Protection" requires protecting data:

options.label: A
options.text: Only while it is displayed on screen

options.label: B
options.text: Throughout its entire lifecycle—creation, processing, storage, and destruction

options.label: C
options.text: Only after a regulator requests it

options.label: D
options.text: Only during the initial collection step

explanation.why_correct: End-to-end security protects data across its full lifecycle: creation, processing, storage, and destruction, with secure handling and transmission.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Protection must extend beyond on-screen display to all lifecycle stages.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Protection is proactive, not triggered by a regulator request.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Protection spans the whole lifecycle, not only collection.

questions.exam_reasoning: Ties end-to-end security to full-lifecycle data protection.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > End-to-End Security – Full Lifecycle Protection

questions.question: The Trusted Computing Base (TCB) is BEST defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: The combination of hardware, software, and controls that work together to enforce a security policy

options.label: B
options.text: A single firewall at the network perimeter

options.label: C
options.text: A precomputed table of password hashes

options.label: D
options.text: The list of all users authorized to access a system

explanation.why_correct: The TCB is the totality of protection mechanisms (hardware, software, firmware, and controls) that together enforce the system's security policy.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A firewall is one control, not the entire trusted computing base.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A user list is not the TCB.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A rainbow table is an attack artifact, unrelated to the TCB.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the TCB definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Understanding Security Models

questions.question: The reference monitor concept describes a component that:

options.label: A
options.text: Physically restricts entry to the server room

options.label: B
options.text: Verifies and enforces access requests between subjects and objects

options.label: C
options.text: Generates cryptographic key pairs in hardware

options.label: D
options.text: Stores backup copies of all system data

explanation.why_correct: The reference monitor mediates (verifies and enforces) all access requests between subjects and objects.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Backups are a recovery function, not the reference monitor.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Key generation is a TPM/HSM function.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Physical entry restriction is a facility control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the reference monitor's mediation role.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Reference Monitor

questions.question: How does the security kernel relate to the reference monitor concept?

options.label: A
options.text: The security kernel is the hardware/software implementation that enforces the reference monitor concept

options.label: B
options.text: The security kernel is an abstract idea while the reference monitor is physical hardware only

options.label: C
options.text: The security kernel replaces the need for any access control

options.label: D
options.text: They are unrelated; the kernel handles only memory paging

explanation.why_correct: The security kernel is the actual implementation (hardware, firmware, software) that realizes and enforces the reference monitor concept, handling access requests and maintaining security integrity.

why_others_are_wrong.B: The reference monitor is the abstract concept; the kernel is its implementation—this option reverses them.
why_others_are_wrong.D: They are directly related, not unrelated.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The kernel enforces access control; it does not eliminate it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the concept (reference monitor) vs implementation (security kernel) relationship.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Security Kernel

questions.question: A "trusted path" provides:

options.label: A
options.text: A precomputed lookup of password hashes

options.label: B
options.text: A protected communication channel between the user and the security functions of a system

options.label: C
options.text: A list of all open network ports

options.label: D
options.text: A magnetic method to destroy data

explanation.why_correct: A trusted path is a protected channel that assures users they are communicating directly with the TCB/security functions, free from interference.

why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes a rainbow table.
why_others_are_wrong.D: That describes degaussing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: That describes a port scan result.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of trusted path as a protected user-to-TCB channel.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Trusted Path

questions.question: A lattice-based access control model assigns security based on:

options.label: A
options.text: The number of CPU cores in the system

options.label: B
options.text: The physical color of the device chassis

options.label: C
options.text: The order in which users logged in

options.label: D
options.text: Levels (and compartments) where each subject/object sits at a defined position with upper and lower bounds

explanation.why_correct: Lattice models place subjects and objects at defined security levels with least-upper-bound/greatest-lower-bound relationships, underpinning models like Biba and Bell-LaPadula.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Login order does not define lattice positions.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Chassis color is irrelevant.
why_others_are_wrong.A: CPU core count is irrelevant to a lattice.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the level/bounds nature of lattice models.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Security Perimeter

questions.question: The Bell-LaPadula model is designed primarily to protect which security property?

explanation.why_correct: Bell-LaPadula is a confidentiality model, especially used in military/government environments.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Integrity is the focus of Biba and Clark-Wilson.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Availability is not the focus of BLP.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Non-repudiation is a cryptographic property, not BLP's focus.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall that BLP = confidentiality.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Bell-LaPadula Model

questions.question: Bell-LaPadula's Simple Security Rule states "no read up." What does its Star (*) Property state?

explanation.why_correct: The BLP Star Property is "no write down"—subjects cannot write to a lower classification, preventing leakage of sensitive data to lower levels.

why_others_are_wrong.A: "No read down" is the Biba Simple Integrity Axiom.
why_others_are_wrong.D: "No write up" is the Biba Star Integrity Axiom.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "No read up" is the BLP Simple Security Rule, not the Star Property.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the BLP star property (no write down).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Bell-LaPadula Model

questions.question: A military system must ensure a user cleared only to "Secret" cannot read "Top Secret" documents. Which model rule directly enforces this, and from which model?

options.label: A
options.text: Simple Integrity Axiom (no read down) — Biba

options.label: B
options.text: Simple Security Rule (no read up) — Bell-LaPadula

options.label: D
options.text: Star Integrity Axiom (no write up) — Biba

explanation.why_correct: Preventing a lower-cleared subject from reading higher-classified data is the Bell-LaPadula Simple Security Rule ("no read up"), a confidentiality protection.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Biba's simple integrity axiom (no read down) protects integrity, not confidentiality of higher data.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Biba's star integrity axiom (no write up) is an integrity rule.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Clark-Wilson well-formed transactions protect integrity in business apps.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps a confidentiality "no read up" requirement to BLP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Bell-LaPadula Model

questions.question: The Biba model is designed primarily to protect:

explanation.why_correct: Biba prioritizes integrity, ensuring the accuracy and consistency of data, and is based on the lattice model.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Confidentiality is the focus of Bell-LaPadula.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Availability is not Biba's focus.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Anonymity is not an addressed property.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall that Biba = integrity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Biba Model

questions.question: Biba's Simple Integrity Axiom is "no read down." What is its Star Integrity Axiom?

explanation.why_correct: Biba's Star Integrity Axiom is "no write up"—lower-integrity subjects cannot write to higher-integrity objects, protecting data integrity.

why_others_are_wrong.A: "No write down" is the Bell-LaPadula star property.
why_others_are_wrong.D: "No read up" is the Bell-LaPadula simple security rule.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "No read down" is Biba's Simple Integrity Axiom, not the star axiom.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the Biba star integrity axiom (no write up).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Biba Model

questions.question: A financial system must ensure low-integrity data entered by untrusted processes cannot corrupt high-integrity records. Which rule applies?

options.label: A
options.text: Biba Star Integrity Axiom (no write up)

options.label: B
options.text: Bell-LaPadula Simple Security Rule (no read up)

explanation.why_correct: Preventing low-integrity subjects from writing to high-integrity objects is Biba's Star Integrity Axiom ("no write up"), protecting record integrity.

why_others_are_wrong.C: BLP no-write-down protects confidentiality, not integrity of high records.
why_others_are_wrong.B: BLP no-read-up is a confidentiality rule.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Brewer-Nash prevents conflicts of interest, not integrity corruption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps integrity protection to Biba's no-write-up rule.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Biba Model

questions.question: Match each security model (1-4) to its primary focus (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Integrity via well-formed transactions and an access triple

options.label: B
options.text: Integrity using a lattice (no read down / no write up)

options.label: C
options.text: Confidentiality (no read up / no write down)

explanation.why_correct: Bell-LaPadula → confidentiality (B); Biba → integrity via lattice (D); Clark-Wilson → integrity via well-formed transactions/access triple (A); Brewer-Nash → conflict-of-interest prevention (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of the major security models to their focus.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Security Models - Part 2

questions.question: The Clark-Wilson model enforces integrity by requiring subjects to access data only through:

options.label: B
options.text: Direct, unrestricted read/write to all objects

options.label: C
options.text: Well-formed transactions via an access triple (subject, program, object)

explanation.why_correct: Clark-Wilson restricts subjects from directly manipulating data; access occurs through programs (the subject-program-object access triple) using well-formed transactions.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Clark-Wilson specifically restricts direct manipulation of data.
why_others_are_wrong.A: No-read-up is a Bell-LaPadula confidentiality rule.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Conflict-of-interest separation is Brewer-Nash.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the Clark-Wilson access triple and well-formed transactions.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Clark-Wilson Model

questions.question: In Clark-Wilson, which element verifies that a Constrained Data Item (CDI) remains in a valid, consistent state after modification?

explanation.why_correct: The Integrity Verification Procedure (IVP) verifies that the integrity of a CDI is maintained after modification.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A Transformation Procedure (TP) is the authorized method that modifies a CDI.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A UDI is data that does not require protection.
why_others_are_wrong.D: An ACM maps subjects to object permissions; it is not the Clark-Wilson IVP.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes IVP (verify) from TP (modify) in Clark-Wilson.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Key Terms

questions.question: A consulting firm must ensure an analyst who accessed Company A's confidential data cannot then access data from Company A's direct competitor. Which model addresses this?

explanation.why_correct: The Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) model dynamically prevents access that would create a conflict of interest, such as accessing competing companies' data.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Bell-LaPadula addresses confidentiality classification levels, not conflicts of interest.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Biba addresses integrity.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Graham-Denning defines subject/object creation and access-rights actions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps conflict-of-interest prevention to Brewer-Nash.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Brewer-Nash Model (Chinese Wall Model)

questions.question: The Graham-Denning model focuses on:

options.label: A
options.text: Preventing low-integrity writes to high-integrity data

options.label: B
options.text: Suppressing fires in a data center

options.label: C
options.text: Enforcing no read up for confidentiality

options.label: D
options.text: Securely creating/deleting subjects and objects and managing access rights via an access control matrix

explanation.why_correct: Graham-Denning defines eight primary actions for securely creating/deleting subjects and objects and granting/transferring/revoking access rights, using an access control matrix.

why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes Biba's star integrity axiom.
why_others_are_wrong.C: That describes Bell-LaPadula's simple security rule.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression is a physical security control, not a model.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of Graham-Denning's focus on subject/object/rights operations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Graham-Denning Model

questions.question: The Take-Grant model uses rules such as take, grant, create, and remove primarily to:

options.label: A
options.text: Detect hash collisions in weak algorithms

options.label: B
options.text: Define classification levels for military data

options.label: C
options.text: Manage how access rights are transferred or revoked between subjects and objects

options.label: D
options.text: Suppress electrical fires in server rooms

explanation.why_correct: Take-Grant uses take, grant, create, and remove rules to model how rights are assigned, inherited, or removed based on trust relationships.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Hash collisions relate to birthday attacks, not Take-Grant.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Classification levels relate to data classification/Bell-LaPadula context, not Take-Grant rules.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the Take-Grant rights-transfer rules.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Biba Model

questions.question: The Sutherland (Non-Deducibility) model aims to prevent which type of security problem?

options.label: B
options.text: Information leaks through covert channels and unauthorized inferences about data

options.label: D
options.text: Excessive humidity in a server room

explanation.why_correct: The Sutherland (Non-Deducibility) model controls information flow to prevent leaks via covert channels and prevent unauthorized inferences about protected data.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Tape theft is a physical security issue.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Hash cracking is a cryptanalytic attack.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Humidity is an environmental control concern.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps covert-channel/inference prevention to Sutherland/non-deducibility.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > Sutherland Model

questions.question: In an access control matrix, the permissions a specific subject has on a specific object are found:

options.label: A

why_others_are_wrong.D: Headers label rows/columns; permissions live in the cells.

questions.question: Within Common Criteria, an Evaluation Assurance Level (EAL) expresses:

options.label: A

options.label: D
options.text: The number of users licensed to use the product

questions.question: The ACID properties that ensure reliable database transactions stand for:

why_others_are_wrong.B: These are not the ACID properties.

questions.question: Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and SCADA environments are especially security-sensitive primarily because:

options.text: They store only public marketing data

options.label: D
options.text: They manage physical processes (e.g., power, water) where a compromise can cause real-world physical impact

why_others_are_wrong.A: Many ICS are networked, increasing exposure.

questions.question: A company is deploying hundreds of inexpensive IoT sensors. Which is the MOST appropriate security consideration for this rollout?

options.label: B
options.text: Disable all monitoring to reduce alert volume

options.label: D
options.text: Segment IoT devices on isolated networks and change default credentials, since many lack strong built-in security

questions.question: A user without access to classified salary data is able to deduce an executive's salary by combining several unclassified query results. This database vulnerability is BEST described as:

questions.question: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) primarily combines:

options.text: Disabling all logging to improve performance

options.label: D
options.text: Securing APIs and inter-service communications with encryption

questions.question: A finite state machine model considers a system secure if:

options.label: A
options.text: It encrypts all data with symmetric keys

options.text: It begins in a secure state and every permitted transition leads to another secure state

options.label: C
options.text: It has the most network ports open

options.label: D
options.text: It uses the fastest possible CPU

explanation.why_correct: In a state machine model, a system is secure if it starts in a secure state and all transitions keep it in secure states.

why_others_are_wrong.D: CPU speed is irrelevant to the model.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Encryption choice is not what defines a secure state machine.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Open ports do not define security in a state machine model.

questions.question: The Non-Interference (Goguen-Meseguer) model ensures that:

options.text: Actions of higher-security subjects do not affect or become visible to lower-security subjects

questions.question: A team is moving many small functions to a serverless (FaaS) platform. Which security concern is MOST characteristic of serverless architectures?

options.label: B
options.text: The need to physically rack and patch their own servers

options.label: C
options.text: Complete elimination of all application vulnerabilities

options.label: D
options.text: An expanded attack surface with reduced control over the underlying environment

explanation.why_correct: Serverless expands the attack surface (many small functions/triggers) and reduces customer control over the environment, complicating traditional security approaches.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Serverless removes server management; there is no physical racking for the customer.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Application code can still contain vulnerabilities.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Misconfiguration remains a major serverless risk.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the characteristic serverless attack-surface/control trade-off.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Risks and Vulnerabilities in Serverless Computing

questions.question: Which is a recommended mitigation for serverless security risk?

options.label: B
options.text: Grant each function unlimited permissions for convenience

options.label: C
options.text: Store all secrets in plaintext within the function code

options.label: D
options.text: Minimize code/microservices and limit the use of sensitive data in functions

explanation.why_correct: Mitigations include clarifying responsibility, minimizing code/microservices, limiting sensitive data use, and designing architecture for CIA.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Unlimited permissions violate least privilege and expand impact.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Disabling monitoring removes detection capability.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Plaintext secrets in code is a severe vulnerability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies sound serverless mitigations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Mitigations for Serverless Computing Security

questions.question: A primary WEAKNESS of symmetric encryption compared to asymmetric encryption is:

options.label: A
options.text: Secure key distribution and scalability of keys among many parties

options.label: C
options.text: It cannot encrypt data at all

options.label: D
options.text: It is far too slow for bulk data encryption

explanation.why_correct: Symmetric encryption is fast but struggles with secure key distribution and scalability (the number of keys grows rapidly as parties increase).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Symmetric encryption is fast and well suited to bulk data—asymmetric is the slower one.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Symmetric encryption does encrypt data.
why_others_are_wrong.B: It requires a shared secret key.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the key-distribution/scalability weakness of symmetric crypto.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Symmetric Encryption

questions.question: Alice wants to send a confidential message to Bob using asymmetric encryption so that only Bob can read it. Alice should encrypt the message with:

options.label: B
options.text: A shared symmetric key sent in the clear

options.label: C
options.text: Bob's public key (so only Bob's private key can decrypt it)

explanation.why_correct: For confidentiality, the sender encrypts with the recipient's public key; only the recipient's matching private key can decrypt it.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Only Bob holds his private key; Alice cannot encrypt with it, and it is not used for inbound confidentiality.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Encrypting with Alice's private key provides a signature, not confidentiality (anyone can decrypt with her public key).
why_others_are_wrong.B: Sending a symmetric key in the clear exposes it to interception.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests using the recipient's public key for confidentiality.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Asymmetric Encryption

questions.question: To create a digital signature that provides integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation, the sender signs a hash of the message with:

explanation.why_correct: A digital signature is created by hashing the message and encrypting the hash with the sender's private key; anyone can verify with the sender's public key, providing integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation.

why_others_are_wrong.A: The recipient's public key is used for confidentiality, not signing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A symmetric key cannot provide non-repudiation (both parties share it).
why_others_are_wrong.B: The sender's public key is used to verify, not create, the signature.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests signing with the sender's private key.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Digital Signatures

questions.question: A cryptographic hash function is primarily used to provide:

explanation.why_correct: A hash function produces a fixed-length one-way digest used to verify integrity—any change to the input changes the hash.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Hashing is one-way and does not provide confidentiality (it is not reversible encryption).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Hashing is not bulk encryption.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Physical access control is unrelated to hashing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps hashing to integrity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Hashing

questions.question: A Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) combines a hash with a secret key to provide:

options.label: B
options.text: Non-repudiation through a public/private key pair

options.label: C
options.text: Confidentiality of the entire message body

options.label: D
options.text: Integrity and authenticity of a message

explanation.why_correct: HMAC uses a shared secret key with a hash to provide message integrity and authenticity; because the key is shared, it does not provide non-repudiation.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Non-repudiation requires asymmetric keys (a digital signature), not a shared HMAC key.
why_others_are_wrong.C: HMAC authenticates/verifies integrity but does not encrypt the message for confidentiality.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Media destruction is unrelated to HMAC.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes HMAC (integrity+authenticity) from digital signatures (add non-repudiation).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC)

questions.question: Storing a copy of cryptographic keys with a trusted third party so they can be recovered if needed is called:

explanation.why_correct: Key escrow places a copy of keys with a trusted third party for recovery (e.g., for lawful access or business continuity).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Key rotation periodically replaces keys with new ones.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Split knowledge divides key components among multiple people.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Key revocation invalidates a key that should no longer be used.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of key escrow.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Cryptographic Key Management

questions.question: A bank requires that no single administrator can reconstruct the master key alone; two of three custodians must combine their key parts. This control is:

explanation.why_correct: Split knowledge divides the key (or its components) among multiple parties so a threshold must cooperate to use/reconstruct it, enforcing dual control.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Key escrow stores a recoverable copy with a third party, not a split-component scheme.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Key rotation replaces keys periodically.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Open design is a secure-design principle, not a key-management control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps M-of-N key reconstruction to split knowledge/dual control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Cryptographic Key Management

questions.question: Periodically replacing cryptographic keys with new ones to limit the impact of a compromised key is:

explanation.why_correct: Key rotation periodically replaces keys, reducing the window and data exposed if a key is compromised.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Key escrow stores recoverable copies of keys.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Split knowledge divides key components among parties.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Frequency analysis is a cryptanalytic technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of key rotation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Cryptographic Key Management

questions.question: In Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), which entity issues and digitally signs digital certificates that bind a public key to an identity?

explanation.why_correct: A Certificate Authority (CA) issues and signs digital certificates binding a public key to a verified identity.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A PEP is a Zero Trust enforcement component.
why_others_are_wrong.B: An HSM stores/protects keys but is not the certificate-issuing authority.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A data steward is a data SME role, not a PKI authority.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the CA's role in PKI.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)

questions.question: Order the following stages of the cryptographic key life cycle from first to last. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: Keys are generated, then distributed/stored securely, used (and rotated) during their validity, and finally revoked/destroyed at end of life.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordering of the cryptographic key life cycle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Cryptographic Life Cycle Steps

questions.question: Order the steps by which a subject obtains and uses a PKI certificate. (Provide the option labels in order.)

options.label: A
options.text: Relying parties validate the certificate (e.g., via CRL/OCSP) before trusting it

options.label: B
options.text: Registration Authority verifies the subject's identity

options.label: C
options.text: Certificate Authority issues and signs the digital certificate

options.label: D
options.text: Subject generates a key pair and submits a certificate signing request

explanation.why_correct: The subject generates keys and submits a CSR, the RA verifies identity, the CA issues/signs the certificate, and relying parties validate it (checking revocation) before trusting it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordered PKI certificate issuance/validation flow.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > PKI Certificate Creation Process

questions.question: The PRIMARY concern about large-scale quantum computers for current cryptography is that they could:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminate the need for any encryption keys

options.label: C
options.text: Make all hashing instantly reversible with no effort

options.label: D
options.text: Break widely used asymmetric algorithms (e.g., RSA) by efficiently solving their underlying math problems

explanation.why_correct: Quantum computers threaten current asymmetric algorithms (such as RSA/ECC) by efficiently solving the hard math problems they rely on, motivating post-quantum cryptography.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Quantum computing weakens some symmetric/hash strength but does not make hashing trivially reversible.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Encryption still requires keys; quantum changes which algorithms are safe.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Quantum computing does not remotely degauss media.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the quantum threat to asymmetric cryptography.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Quantum Cryptography

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are SYMMETRIC encryption algorithms/standards? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: AES and 3DES are symmetric ciphers that use the same key to encrypt and decrypt.

why_others_are_wrong.C: RSA is an asymmetric algorithm.
why_others_are_wrong.D: ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) is asymmetric.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes symmetric ciphers from asymmetric algorithms.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Symmetric Encryption

questions.question: Which TWO are genuine key-management risks that weaken a cryptosystem? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Rotating keys on a defined schedule

options.label: D
options.text: Revoking keys that are known to be compromised

explanation.why_correct: Weak/short keys and insecure key storage/usage are key-management risks; rotation and revocation of compromised keys are good practices, not risks.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Scheduled key rotation is a protective practice, not a risk.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Revoking compromised keys is a protective practice, not a risk.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates key-management weaknesses from sound practices.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Key Management Risks

questions.question: Why does symmetric encryption alone NOT provide non-repudiation?

options.label: A
options.text: Symmetric keys are too long to manage

options.label: C
options.text: Symmetric algorithms are always broken by quantum computers

options.label: D
options.text: Both parties share the same secret key, so neither can prove the other was the sole originator

explanation.why_correct: Because the same secret key is shared, either party could have produced a message, so symmetric encryption cannot prove sole origin (no non-repudiation); digital signatures (asymmetric) are needed.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Key length is not the reason non-repudiation fails.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Symmetric encryption does protect confidentiality.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Quantum impact is separate from the non-repudiation limitation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Explains why shared keys preclude non-repudiation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Virtualization and Cloud Computing > Symmetric Encryption

questions.question: A brute-force attack against a cipher works by:

options.label: A
options.text: Tricking a user into revealing their password

options.label: B
options.text: Analyzing the power consumption of the device

options.label: C
options.text: Trying all possible key combinations until the correct one is found

explanation.why_correct: Brute force tries every possible key; given enough time and resources it is guaranteed to succeed, which is why sufficient key length matters.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Analyzing power consumption is a side-channel attack.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Reusing a captured token is a replay attack.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Tricking a user is social engineering.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of brute force as exhaustive key search.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Summary of Key Attacks

questions.question: In a known-plaintext attack, the attacker attempts to recover the key by analyzing:

options.label: A
options.text: Known plaintext together with its corresponding ciphertext

options.label: C
options.text: A precomputed table of password hashes

options.label: D
options.text: Only ciphertext, with no plaintext available

explanation.why_correct: A known-plaintext attack uses pairs of known plaintext and its resulting ciphertext to deduce the key.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Having only ciphertext describes a ciphertext-only attack.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Electromagnetic emissions are exploited by side-channel attacks.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Precomputed hash tables describe a rainbow table attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes known-plaintext from ciphertext-only attacks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Cryptanalytic Attacks - Part 1

questions.question: A chosen-plaintext attack is characterized by the attacker's ability to:

options.label: A
options.text: Select specific plaintext, have it encrypted, and analyze the resulting ciphertext

options.label: D
options.text: Only observe ciphertext that happens to be transmitted

explanation.why_correct: In a chosen-plaintext attack, the attacker chooses plaintext, obtains its ciphertext, and analyzes the pair to narrow down the key.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Passive observation of ciphertext is a ciphertext-only attack.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Destroying hardware is not a cryptanalytic chosen-plaintext attack.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Reusing tokens is a replay attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the chosen-plaintext capability.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Chosen Plaintext Attack

questions.question: Which attack attempts to discover the key by analyzing ONLY ciphertext, with no access to matching plaintext?

explanation.why_correct: A ciphertext-only attack works from ciphertext alone, often aided by techniques like frequency analysis.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Known-plaintext requires matching plaintext-ciphertext pairs.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Chosen-plaintext requires the attacker to encrypt chosen plaintext.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A replay attack reuses captured messages, not pure ciphertext analysis.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ciphertext-only definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Cryptanalytic Attacks - Part 2

questions.question: Differential cryptanalysis attempts to recover key information by:

options.label: B
options.text: Analyzing how small differences in plaintext (or key) affect the resulting ciphertext

options.label: C
options.text: Capturing and replaying a valid message

options.label: D
options.text: Measuring the time each operation takes

explanation.why_correct: Differential cryptanalysis studies how slight changes (differences) in plaintext or key propagate to ciphertext to infer key information.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Exhaustive key search is brute force.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Measuring operation time is a timing/side-channel attack.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Capturing and replaying is a replay attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the differential-analysis concept.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Chosen Plaintext Attack

questions.question: A meet-in-the-middle attack is particularly effective against ciphers that:

options.label: A
options.text: Use only a single short key with no rounds

options.label: D
options.text: Use multiple rounds/stages of encryption (e.g., double encryption)

explanation.why_correct: Meet-in-the-middle encrypts from one end and decrypts from the other to find matching intermediate values, making it effective against multi-stage (e.g., double) encryption.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Single-stage short-key ciphers are attacked by brute force, not meet-in-the-middle.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Air-gapping is a physical control unrelated to this cryptanalytic method.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Encryption inherently involves a key.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the multi-stage target of meet-in-the-middle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Meet in the Middle Attack

questions.question: An attacker finds two different inputs that produce the SAME hash value to bypass an integrity check on a weak hashing algorithm. This exploits which attack?

options.label: A
options.text: Brute force of a symmetric key

explanation.why_correct: A birthday attack exploits the birthday paradox to find hash collisions (two inputs with the same hash), undermining integrity controls on weaker hash algorithms.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A replay attack reuses captured messages.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A side-channel attack measures physical characteristics.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Brute-forcing a symmetric key is not about hash collisions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps hash collisions to the birthday attack.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Hash-Based Attacks

questions.question: A rainbow table attack recovers passwords by:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypting chosen plaintext and analyzing the output

options.label: C
options.text: Matching a captured password hash against precomputed hash-to-plaintext tables

explanation.why_correct: A rainbow table uses precomputed tables of hashes for common passwords; a captured hash matching an entry reveals the plaintext password (salting defends against this).

why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes a chosen-plaintext attack.
why_others_are_wrong.D: That describes a timing/side-channel attack.
why_others_are_wrong.B: That describes session replay.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the precomputed-hash nature of rainbow tables.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Hash-Based Attacks

questions.question: An attacker steals NTLM password hashes from a Windows host and uses them directly to authenticate to other systems without ever cracking the plaintext password. This is:

explanation.why_correct: Pass the hash uses stolen password hashes directly for authentication, commonly targeting Windows LM/NTLM, without needing the plaintext password.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Kerberoasting targets Kerberos tickets, not NTLM hash reuse.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A birthday attack finds hash collisions, not credential reuse.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A timing attack measures operation duration.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recognition of pass-the-hash.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Hash-Based Attacks

questions.question: Kerberoasting specifically targets:

options.label: B
options.text: The power consumption of a smart card

options.label: C
options.text: Physical badge readers at a facility

options.label: D
options.text: Kerberos authentication by harvesting and cracking service ticket hashes

explanation.why_correct: Kerberoasting targets Kerberos by requesting and harvesting service-ticket hashes and attempting to crack them offline to obtain credentials.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Power consumption is a side-channel target.
why_others_are_wrong.A: CRLs relate to PKI certificate validation, not Kerberoasting.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Badge readers are physical controls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps Kerberos ticket cracking to Kerberoasting.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Hash-Based Attacks

questions.question: An attacker intercepts an encrypted authentication message and resends it later to gain access. Which countermeasure BEST defends against this replay attack?

options.label: D
options.text: Timestamps, expiration periods, or nonces/timeouts on messages

explanation.why_correct: Replay attacks reuse captured valid messages; timestamps, expiration windows, and nonces/timeouts ensure a captured message cannot be reused later.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Fences are physical perimeter controls, irrelevant to message replay.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fire suppression is a facility control.
why_others_are_wrong.A: CPU speed has no effect on replay defense.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps anti-replay measures (timestamps/nonces) to replay attacks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Replay Attack

questions.question: An attacker measures the exact time and power a smart card uses during cryptographic operations to infer the secret key, without attacking the algorithm mathematically. This is a:

explanation.why_correct: Side-channel attacks exploit physical operational characteristics (timing, power consumption, emissions) rather than the math of the algorithm; timing analysis is one variant.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A chosen-ciphertext attack analyzes selected ciphertext and its decryption, not physical characteristics.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Brute force tries all keys mathematically.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A man-in-the-middle intercepts communications between parties.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests recognition of side-channel/timing attacks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Side Channel Attack

questions.question: In cryptanalysis, "work factor" refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: The humidity level in the server room

options.label: B
options.text: The time, effort, and resources required to break a cryptosystem

options.label: C
options.text: The physical weight of the cryptographic hardware

options.label: D
options.text: The number of employees who manage the system

explanation.why_correct: Work factor measures the effort/time/resources needed to defeat a cryptosystem, helping assess whether an attack is feasible.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Staff count is unrelated to work factor.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Physical weight is irrelevant.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Humidity is an environmental control concern.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the work-factor concept.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Cryptanalytic Attacks - Part 3

questions.question: Match each cryptanalytic attack (1-4) to its description (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Reuses a captured valid message to gain access

options.label: B
options.text: Exploits physical characteristics such as timing or power use

options.label: C
options.text: Tries all possible keys until one works

options.label: D
options.text: Finds two inputs producing the same hash (collision)

explanation.why_correct: Brute force → tries all keys (B); Birthday → hash collision (A); Side-channel → physical characteristics (D); Replay → reuses captured message (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of cryptanalytic attacks to their mechanisms.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Summary of Attacks

questions.question: Which TWO attacks specifically target password HASHES? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Rainbow table attacks and pass-the-hash both target password hashes (matching precomputed hashes, and reusing stolen hashes respectively).

why_others_are_wrong.A: CPTED is a physical site-design strategy, not a hash attack.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A brownout is a power anomaly, not a hash attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies hash-targeting attacks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Hash-Based Attacks

questions.question: Which TWO techniques are associated with analyzing ciphertext to break encryption? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Frequency analysis (identifying repeating patterns) and related-key attacks (comparing ciphertexts under related keys) are ciphertext-focused cryptanalytic techniques.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A mantrap is a physical access control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Generator maintenance is a power-availability practice.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates ciphertext cryptanalysis from physical controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Cryptanalytic Attacks > Cryptanalytic Attacks - Part 2

questions.question: Physical security is often described as the ________ in protecting sensitive data, systems, and personnel.

explanation.why_correct: Physical security is the first line of defense, protecting facilities, systems, and people before logical controls are even reached.

why_others_are_wrong.C: It is a primary, front-line defense, not merely a last resort.
why_others_are_wrong.B: It is foundational, not least important.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Encryption is a logical control; physical security is distinct.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of physical security as the first line of defense.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Physical Security

questions.question: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) focuses on:

options.label: A
options.text: Designing the physical environment to influence behavior and deter crime

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypting data at rest on servers

explanation.why_correct: CPTED uses environmental design (natural access control, surveillance, and territorial reinforcement) to influence behavior and deter crime.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Encryption is a logical control, not CPTED.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Key generation is a cryptographic function.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Shared responsibility is a cloud concept.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of CPTED's purpose.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED)

questions.question: Which TWO are key elements of CPTED? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: CPTED elements are natural access control, natural surveillance, and natural territorial reinforcement.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Pre-action sprinklers are a fire suppression system, not a CPTED element.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Rainbow tables are a cryptanalytic attack technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies genuine CPTED elements.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED)

questions.question: Designing a parking lot with clear sightlines and good lighting so that activity is easily observed is an example of which CPTED element?

explanation.why_correct: Natural surveillance designs spaces (lighting, sightlines) so legitimate users can readily observe activity, deterring crime.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Natural access control guides movement via design (paths, entrances).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Natural territorial reinforcement uses design to express ownership of space.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A mantrap is a specific physical access control device, not a CPTED element.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps sightlines/lighting to natural surveillance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED)

questions.question: To deter a DETERMINED intruder, the guide recommends fencing of approximately:

explanation.why_correct: Fencing of 8+ feet with barbed wire is intended to deter determined intruders; 3-4 feet only deters casual trespassers.

why_others_are_wrong.A: 3-4 feet deters only casual intruders.
why_others_are_wrong.C: 1 foot edging provides no meaningful deterrence.
why_others_are_wrong.D: No fence provides no perimeter deterrence.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests fence-height deterrence guidance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Types of Physical Security Controls

questions.question: A data center wants to prevent an unauthorized person from slipping in behind an authorized employee (tailgating). Which control DIRECTLY addresses this?

options.label: A
options.text: A mantrap (double-door interlock allowing one person at a time)

explanation.why_correct: A mantrap uses interlocking doors that admit one person at a time, directly preventing tailgating/piggybacking into secure areas.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A fence addresses perimeter intrusion, not tailgating at a door.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A sprinkler is fire suppression.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A generator provides backup power.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps anti-tailgating at entry to a mantrap.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Types of Physical Security Controls

questions.question: Sturdy posts installed in front of a building entrance to stop a vehicle from ramming into it are called:

explanation.why_correct: Bollards are posts/barriers that prevent vehicles from ramming into a structure or pedestrian area.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Turnstiles control pedestrian flow, not vehicle ramming.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A mantrap prevents tailgating at a door.
why_others_are_wrong.C: PTZ cameras are surveillance devices.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of bollards as anti-vehicle barriers.

questions.question: Which TWO are categories of facility security controls described in the guide's layered (defense-in-depth) approach? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Facility controls follow a layered model of deterrence, denial, detection, delay, and response; deterrence and delay are two of these categories.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Kerberoasting is a cryptanalytic credential attack.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Brute force is a cryptanalytic attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies genuine facility control categories.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Types of Facility Security Controls

questions.question: A Passive Infrared (PIR) sensor detects intruders by sensing:

options.label: A
options.text: Changes in infrared (heat) energy from a moving body

explanation.why_correct: A PIR sensor detects the infrared (heat) energy changes caused by a moving person, a common motion-detection method.

why_others_are_wrong.D: RFI relates to electrical noise, not PIR motion detection.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Voltage fluctuations are power anomalies, not PIR triggers.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Hash collisions are a cryptographic concept.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of PIR (heat-based) detection.

questions.question: Among the four data center tiers, which provides the HIGHEST uptime and redundancy?

explanation.why_correct: Data center Tier 4 provides the highest level of uptime and redundancy; Tier 1 is the lowest.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Tier 1 has the lowest uptime/redundancy.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Tier 2 is below Tier 3 and Tier 4.
why_others_are_wrong.D: "Tier 0" is not a data center tier.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of Tier 4 as highest availability.
