questions.question: Server room humidity is generally kept around 50% because excessively LOW humidity can cause:

explanation.why_correct: Low humidity increases static electricity (ESD risk), while high humidity causes condensation and metal corrosion—so ~50% is targeted.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Corrosion results from HIGH humidity, not low.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Power surges are an electrical anomaly, not a humidity effect.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Hash collisions are a cryptographic concept.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests low-humidity (static) vs high-humidity (corrosion) effects.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > HVAC Considerations

questions.question: An EXTENDED period of low voltage (not a complete outage) is called a:

explanation.why_correct: A brownout is an extended period of low voltage; a sag is a temporary (brief) low voltage.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A sag is a temporary (short) low voltage, not extended.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A blackout is a complete power loss.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A spike is a temporary high voltage.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes brownout (extended low) from sag (temporary low).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Power Issues

questions.question: A momentary (very brief) increase in voltage is a spike, whereas an EXTENDED period of high voltage is a:

explanation.why_correct: A surge is an extended period of high voltage; a spike is a temporary (momentary) high voltage.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A sag is a temporary low voltage.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A brownout is an extended low voltage.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A fault is a temporary power loss.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes surge (extended high) from spike (temporary high).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Power Issues

questions.question: Which TWO terms describe a COMPLETE or temporary LOSS of power (rather than a voltage level change)? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: A blackout is a complete power loss and a fault is a temporary power loss; surge and brownout are voltage-level anomalies, not losses.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A surge is extended HIGH voltage, not a loss.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A brownout is extended LOW voltage, not a complete loss.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates power-loss terms from voltage-level anomalies.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Power Issues

questions.question: The fire triangle consists of heat, fuel, and:

explanation.why_correct: The fire triangle is oxygen, heat, and fuel; removing any one component disrupts the fire.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Water is a suppression agent, not a fire-triangle component.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Humidity is an environmental factor, not a triangle component.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Voltage is a power concept, not part of the fire triangle.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the fire triangle components.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Fire Triangle Components

questions.question: A fire breaks out in energized electrical equipment (Class C). Which suppression agent is appropriate, and which must be AVOIDED?

options.label: A
options.text: Use carbon dioxide or a halon substitute; avoid water

options.label: B
options.text: Use soda acid; avoid halon substitutes

options.label: D
options.text: Use dry powder only; avoid all gases

explanation.why_correct: Class C (electrical) fires require non-conductive agents like carbon dioxide or a halon substitute; water is conductive and dangerous on energized equipment.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Water is conductive and hazardous on electrical fires—this is reversed.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Dry powder is for Class D (metal) fires, not the recommended Class C agent.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Soda acid (water-based) is for Class A, not energized electrical fires.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests correct agent selection for electrical (Class C) fires.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Fire Extinguisher Classes and Materials

questions.question: Which extinguishing agent is appropriate for a Class D (combustible metals such as magnesium or lithium) fire?

explanation.why_correct: Class D combustible-metal fires require dry powder agents; water and common agents can react dangerously with burning metals.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Water can react violently with burning metals.
why_others_are_wrong.B: CO2 is for Class B/C, not Class D metals.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Soda acid is a water-based Class A agent.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps metal fires to dry powder.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Fire Extinguisher Classes and Materials

questions.question: A data center wants a sprinkler system that minimizes the risk of accidental water discharge onto equipment by requiring two separate triggers before water is released. Which system fits BEST?

explanation.why_correct: A pre-action system combines dry and wet pipe behavior and requires two activation conditions (e.g., heat/smoke detection plus sprinkler activation), reducing accidental discharge—suited to computer rooms/data centers.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A deluge system releases large volumes quickly and is not recommended for electronics.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A wet-pipe system is always water-filled, raising accidental-discharge risk.
why_others_are_wrong.D: An open-head (wet) system does not provide the dual-trigger protection.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps dual-trigger, low-accidental-discharge needs to pre-action systems.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Facility-Level Fire Suppression Systems

questions.question: A dry-pipe fire suppression system differs from a wet-pipe system in that the dry-pipe system:

options.label: A
options.text: Is always filled with water ready to discharge immediately

options.label: B
options.text: Requires no water source at all

options.label: D
options.text: Holds compressed air in the pipes and fills with water only upon activation

explanation.why_correct: A dry-pipe system keeps compressed air in the pipes and admits water only when activated, reducing the risk of leaks/freezing compared to an always-charged wet-pipe system.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Being always water-filled describes a wet-pipe (closed-head) system.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Dry-pipe systems still use water, not only CO2.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A water source is still required; it just fills on activation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes dry-pipe (air, fills on activation) from wet-pipe.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Facility-Level Fire Suppression Systems

questions.question: A photoelectric smoke detector triggers based on:

options.label: A
options.text: Disruption of an electrical plate by ionized particles from radioactive material

options.label: B
options.text: Disruption of a light source/beam by smoke particles

options.label: C
options.text: A fixed temperature threshold being reached

options.label: D
options.text: A rapid rate of temperature increase

explanation.why_correct: A photoelectric smoke detector triggers when smoke disrupts a light source/beam; ionization detectors instead use radioactive material affecting an electrical plate.

why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes an ionization smoke detector.
why_others_are_wrong.D: That describes a rate-of-rise heat detector.
why_others_are_wrong.C: That describes a fixed-temperature detector.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes photoelectric from ionization smoke detection.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Fire Detection Methods

questions.question: In fire safety planning, the TOP priority is always to:

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid triggering any alarms to prevent panic

options.label: B
options.text: Protect system assets and equipment above all else

options.label: D
options.text: Protect human life by enabling safe exit from the facility

explanation.why_correct: Protecting human life (safe egress) is the top fire-safety priority; protecting assets is secondary.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Asset protection is secondary to life safety.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Aesthetics are irrelevant to fire safety priorities.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Alarms are essential for safe evacuation, not to be suppressed.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces life safety as the top fire priority.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Physical Security > Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression

questions.question: Managing the information system lifecycle securely means that security should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Added only when an auditor requests it

options.label: C
options.text: Integrated from initiation through disposal, at every phase

options.label: D
options.text: Considered only after the system goes live

explanation.why_correct: Secure lifecycle management integrates security at every phase—from initiation/requirements through development, operations, and secure disposal.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Bolting on security after go-live is reactive and leaves gaps.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Security is proactive, not auditor-triggered.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Security spans the whole lifecycle, not only disposal.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces full-lifecycle security integration.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > System Security Capabilities

questions.question: A server holding sensitive data is being retired at the end of the system lifecycle. Which action is MOST important during this disposal phase?

options.label: A
options.text: Donate the drives immediately without any wiping

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the data intact in case it is needed later

options.label: C
options.text: Publish the data publicly to clear the storage

options.label: D
options.text: Securely sanitize/destroy the data so it cannot be recovered before disposing of the hardware

explanation.why_correct: Secure disposal requires sanitizing or destroying data so it cannot be recovered, then disposing of hardware appropriately.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Leaving sensitive data intact on retired hardware risks disclosure.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Donating un-wiped drives exposes sensitive data (remanence).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Publishing the data is a severe confidentiality breach.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps end-of-life data sanitization to secure disposal.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 3 > Secure Design Principles > System Security Capabilities

questions.question: During the verification and validation stage of the system lifecycle, the goal is to:

options.label: B
options.text: Securely destroy all of the system's data

options.label: C
options.text: Identify and engage stakeholders for the first time

options.label: D
options.text: Confirm through testing/assessment that the system meets its technical, security, and user requirements

explanation.why_correct: Verification and validation use testing, code reviews, and security assessments to confirm the system meets all requirements before full-scale implementation.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Data destruction occurs at disposal/retirement.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Stakeholder engagement is part of initiation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Procurement negotiation is part of acquisition.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps requirement-confirmation testing to verification and validation.
